title: Where Recognition Breaks
scopeNote: This keeps the forward simulation: place a difficulty at one component and read the profile it produces. A sixth component, covert recognition, and the backwards inference from a profile to the component stay in the longer version.
summary: A five-step model of recognising a person, with expression branching off early. Impairing any one step produces a distinct profile of which questions can still be answered, and all five profiles differ.
learningObjectives: Describe recognising a person as an ordered sequence with a branch, not a single ability.
Predict which questions survive an impairment at a given step.
Distinguish an inability to recognise a face from an inability to name a known person.
Explain why reading expression can survive an impairment that destroys identification.
State what a box-and-arrow model is evidence for and what it is not.
interactionTypes: a six-way switch placing the impairment
a model diagram redrawn with the impaired step marked
five questions answered or not, each with its reason
a distinct profile for every impairment, none of them simply worse at faces
a guided case showing the profile the word usually refers to
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with the impairment chosen by a labelled radio group rather than by clicking the diagram, and the guided button moving the radio as well as the drawing. An impaired step is drawn with a broken outline and a cross as well as a colour. The diagram carries a description naming the sequence, the branch, the impaired step and every question that fails, so the profile is fully available as text. Each question tile says can or cannot in words and gives its reason, listing the steps it needs. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: A model, not a patient. No real person is described.
simulationNotes: A question is answerable when every step it needs is intact. Perception, familiarity, identity and name run in order, so impairing one fails everything downstream; expression branches off after perception, which is why it survives an impairment that destroys identification but not one at perception itself. All five impairments produce different profiles, which is the property the model is being judged on. The caution states that a box-and-arrow model summarises which abilities come apart rather than mapping anything in the brain, that a neat sequence overstates how orderly the process is, that familiarity and identity are not cleanly separable in practice, and that developmental prosopagnosia fits a single-step story poorly.
readmeTopic: why recognising a face, knowing who someone is, and producing their name can fail separately
